title: Imperialism: The Highest Stage of Capitalism
author: Vladimir Ilyich Lenin
edition_analyzed: Standard English edition (Penguin Classics, 2010; originally published in Russian, 1917)
target_audience: Students of political science and economics
Readers interested in critiques of capitalism and imperialism
core_themes: Imperialism as the inevitable development of mature capitalism
The relationship between capitalism, monopolies, and global expansion
The consolidation of financial capital and economic domination
Theoretical critique of colonialism and global inequality
Economic rivalry and its role in causing wars
primary_purpose: To analyze the economic and political dynamics of late-stage capitalism, arguing that imperialism is not a policy but a structural phase in capitalist evolution—characterized by monopolies, the dominance of finance capital, and the division and re-division of the world among capitalist powers.

structure_format.organization: Divided into ten chapters, with each chapter addressing a specific aspect or stage of economic development
features: Theoretical explanations with historical and contemporary (early 20th-century) examples
Direct polemic against reformist or revisionist Marxist thinkers

key_concepts_lessons: Imperialism is the monopoly stage of capitalism, marked by the dominance of a small group of powerful corporations and banks.
The export of capital, rather than goods, becomes central to advanced capitalist economies.
Finance capital merges industrial and banking capital, leading to the rise of powerful oligarchies.
Economic territories are divided among capitalist powers, leading to rivalry and conflict.
Imperialism perpetuates economic exploitation, both of other countries and of the working class.
Reformist approaches fail to address the structural roots of imperialism—only revolutionary change can do so.
notable_features: Systematic application of Marxist theory to early 20th-century global affairs
Use of contemporary economic and political data
Critique of both capitalist and revisionist socialist positions
Foreword situating the analysis within the context of World War I
cultural_historical_context: Written during World War I, this work reflects the intense global rivalries among imperialist powers, the spread of colonial empires, and the debates within the socialist movement about war and capitalism. Lenin wrote the book while in exile, intending it as both a theoretical contribution and a guide for revolutionary strategy.
reception_impact: Significantly influenced anti-colonial and anti-imperial movements in the 20th century
Cited by revolutionary leaders worldwide, including in China, Vietnam, and Africa
Criticized by some scholars for economic determinism and for underestimating the adaptability of capitalism
Remains a reference point in debates on globalization, neo-colonialism, and economic inequality
comparable_titles: The Accumulation of Capital by Rosa Luxemburg
Open Veins of Latin America by Eduardo Galeano
The Wretched of the Earth by Frantz Fanon
Globalization and Its Discontents by Joseph Stiglitz
